items.t: Can You Still Buy Accenture Stock Today?
sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Accenture (ACN) stock returned 47.3% in the three months to November 6, 2026, while the S&P 500 lost 4.6%. The shares closed that day at $260.5, leaving them just 7.1% below their January high and putting buyers near the peak price of the past year. Over the full year, however, the stock returned 8.8%, tracking closely with the index’s 9.8%. After a run that fast, is Accenture stock still priced reasonably for what the company earns?

Looking at earnings, yes. Accenture trades at 18.7 times its earnings over the last twelve months, compared with 21.8 for the S&P 500. That multiple climbed quickly. On September 30, right before the shares jumped in October, it sat at 13.2, marking the second lowest of the 40 fiscal quarter-end readings since fiscal 2017. It previously peaked at 42.3 in fiscal Q1 2022.

Margins sit near their best, meaning the below-market multiple is not a sign of a less profitable business. Over the last twelve months, Accenture reported an operating margin of 15.8%, higher than at 38 of those 40 quarter ends. What has changed is Accenture’s growth. Full-year revenue growth came in at 6.5% in fiscal 2026, down from 21.9% in fiscal 2022. Management said organic growth, which leaves out acquisitions, was about 3% in fiscal 2026. Buyers are now paying a lower multiple for a business growing more slowly, part of it through acquisitions.

Analysts are counting on a quarter at the top of management’s guide. They expect sales of $19.6 billion for the first quarter of fiscal 2027, matching the top end of the company’s guide of $18.95 billion to $19.6 billion. Accenture already beat its own guide in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, when management said sales of $18.7 billion came in above the top end of its guided range.

Repeating that performance depends on client spending. Management said the top of its fiscal 2027 range allows for discretionary spending that is stable to slightly improving, while the bottom allows for it to get worse. For fiscal 2027, management expects revenue growth of 3% to 6% in local currency. It also said Accenture saw lower pricing in many areas of its business in the fourth quarter.

Accenture stock faces AI execution test as CIO survey flags value gap
sum: Accenture's CIO Pulse survey puts the consulting group's artificial-intelligence strategy against a tougher execution test: Enterprise AI deployment is spreading, but measurable business returns are not keeping pace. The research was published on November 3, 2026, and draws on responses from 300 chief information officers and senior technology leaders at organizations with more than 1 billion US dollars in revenue.

Accenture said 64% of respondents were scaling enterprise AI deployment, while only 7% had reached optimization at scale. The gap is also visible in how companies use the technology. Seventy percent primarily apply AI to individual productivity and copilots within workflows, compared with 37% using agents for end-to-end orchestration across connected tasks.

The study identifies execution barriers that matter for Accenture's growth prospects. Governance, risk and responsible-AI concerns were cited by 54% of respondents as a top obstacle to scaling AI, while only 32% said their organizations had reached advanced or leading AI-governance maturity. Workforce adoption and training were identified as the biggest execution barrier by 53%.

Enterprise architecture presents another gap. Although 61% of CIOs expect significant transformation or a fundamental redesign of enterprise architecture within three years, only 27% currently include agentic architecture in that redesign. Accenture's findings also show that 65% view AI-native platforms as disruptive or transformative to traditional enterprise software.

The budget outlook points toward a shift rather than an unrestricted spending cycle. CIOs expect the share of IT budgets devoted to core operations to fall from 48% to 41% over the next two years, while spending on innovation and AI is expected to rise from 28% to 39%. Responsible-AI compliance ranks as the top priority for the next 12 to 24 months at 36%, narrowly ahead of scaling AI and driving growth and innovation, both at 33%.
The findings support Accenture's positioning as an implementation partner for enterprise AI, but they also underline the conversion risk facing the business.

sum: Banco de Bogotá's board appointed María Fernanda Suárez Londoño as president on Friday, October 30, after accepting Juan Carlos Echeverry Garzón's resignation. The Rio Times reported the change on Saturday, October 31.

The appointment is a governance development for a bank within one of Colombia's largest financial groups. Any effect on earnings, lending growth or shareholder returns will depend on later strategic and financial decisions rather than on the appointment alone.

PLTR vs. ACN: Which Leading Tech Stock Should You Consider?
sum: Both are major players in the enterprise technology and AI space, with Palantir Technologies PLTR focusing on advanced data and AI-driven software platforms and Accenture plc ACN operating as a global IT services and consulting powerhouse deeply involved in digital transformation and AI deployments.

While Palantir specializes in developing cutting-edge platforms such as Foundry, Gotham, and AIP to empower organizations with data-driven intelligence and decision-making capabilities, Accenture integrates AI across industries through its consulting expertise, cloud capabilities, and vast client network. Together, they represent two complementary forces in the AI ecosystem, one providing transformative technology and the other driving large-scale adoption.

One of Palantir’s most important competitive advantages is its Ontology framework. Rather than treating enterprise information as disconnected data points, the platform models an organization around the real-world assets, customers, orders, facilities and operational relationships that define its business.

This structure allows applications to act on enterprise information within established rules, permissions and workflows. As a result, Palantir is positioned to become more than an analytics vendor. Its software can operate as a digital foundation connecting data, decisions and business processes.

The investment case becomes particularly compelling as artificial intelligence adoption expands. More capable AI models alone do not guarantee meaningful business outcomes. Enterprises still need systems that connect models with trusted data, workflows and controlled actions. Palantir’s Artificial Intelligence Platform, or AIP, addresses this gap by helping organizations deploy AI within operational environments rather than keeping it confined to experimental applications.

Once a customer builds its initial use case around Palantir’s platform, additional applications can be created on the same underlying structure. This potentially improves returns on the original implementation while increasing the difficulty and cost of replacing the platform.
Another potential catalyst lies in Palantir’s deployment model.

Accenture’s last results came on June 18, the day this run began, and it has not reported a quarter since.
Accenture’s Last Report Was Cautious About The Quarter Ahead

In fiscal Q3 2026, revenue grew 3% in local currency, and a couple of large managed services opportunities moved into fiscal 2027. Management then guided fiscal Q4 2026 to growth of 1% to 5% in local currency, and said more of that range was in play because of macro uncertainty. A range that wide is a company saying it cannot see fiscal Q4 2026 clearly.

None of that explains the size of the move. Cognizant (CTSH) rose 42% over the same stretch and Booz Allen Hamilton (BAH) rose 19%, while IBM fell 4%, which reads as the market repricing consulting work rather than Accenture’s execution. What that June report did change is where Accenture is spending its money.

Management said it would deploy about $9 billion on acquisitions in fiscal 2026. Much of it is going where the firm has not competed hard before. It has launched Accenture Edge to sell to the mid-market, an addressable market management sizes at $240 billion. In August it agreed to buy McCoy, a Dutch SAP transformation partner for mid-market companies, and COMWARE in Tokyo, to strengthen Accenture Edge.

Discretionary spending at large enterprises has been the industry’s soft spot for a few years, by management’s own account, and smaller clients are where it wants to make that up. The other big move is OT security: three acquisitions announced with the June results, anchored by a majority stake in a platform that protects the operational technology behind power grids and pipelines. Management says those three acquisitions more than triple the OT security market it can sell into, and it is building a platform business rather than a headcount business.

Not through margins. Accenture’s operating margin over the last twelve months is 15.8%, below the 18.7% median for the S&P 500. Because the growth slowed. Management cut its fiscal 2026 revenue guide to 3% to 4% growth in local currency. The Middle East conflict cost about $100 million of revenue against expectations in fiscal Q3 2026, and a couple of large managed services deals slipped into FY 2027. The stock has fallen 28.9% over the past twelve months while the S&P 500 returned 18.5%, and revenue did not fall at all.

sum: The consulting giant is quietly using its balance sheet to buy its way into entirely new, product-led markets that could redefine its growth story.

If you’ve glanced at Accenture (ACN) stock lately, you might be tempted to just keep walking. It has returned -49% over the past year, a painful drop for a name once seen as a steady compounder. While the market frets over near-term consulting headwinds and delayed deals, management is making a much bigger, more interesting move. They’re going shopping.

In its most recent quarter, Accenture announced it now expects to deploy approximately $9 billion of capital this year. To put that in perspective, this figure was initially $5 billion in acquisitions, which has now been revised to $9 billion. This isn’t just a minor budget increase; it’s a signal of a deliberate, aggressive strategy to buy, not just build, its next phase of growth. The company is actively hunting for assets in higher-growth areas, and it’s putting serious capital to work to get them.

This isn’t about rolling up smaller consulting shops. Look at the company’s big new push into operational technology (OT) security. Accenture recently acquired a trio of companies, Dragos, runZero, and NetRise, to create a security platform. Management is clear about the goal: to build a “platform-led growth business with a non-FTE commercial model.” This is a fundamental shift away from relying solely on billable hours. More importantly, they believe this investment “more than triples our total addressable market in OT security,” a space management says is growing at a double-digit rate. As one executive put it, “We cannot have an AI revolution without critical infrastructure,” and that infrastructure needs to be secure.

The expansion doesn’t stop there. Accenture is also launching a new business called Accenture Edge, aimed squarely at the mid-market. The company estimates this segment of companies with revenue between $300 million and $3 billion represents a “$240 billion addressable market for us, growing high single digits.” This is a concerted effort to capture a large client base that has traditionally been outside its core focus, creating another entirely new avenue for growth. sum: With shares beaten down by a cautious outlook, one number reveals a surprising resilience in the company’s most important deals.

Accenture (ACN)’s stock has had a difficult year. Shares are down 55% over the last 12 months, and the company recently trimmed its revenue forecast, fueling concerns about a broad slowdown in corporate spending. The stock’s price-to-earnings multiple of 10.1 now sits far below its 10-year range of 15.6 to 41.1, suggesting the market has priced in a period of significant weakness.
But in the latest earnings call, a single data point challenges this narrative. It’s a number that points not to weakness, but to strength with the company’s largest and most strategic customers.
Year-to-date, Accenture has signed 104 clients to deals with quarterly bookings over $100 million.

That figure represents a 13% increase over the same period last year. While the market has focused on near-term headwinds, Accenture is securing more of the largest, most complex transformation projects available. Management calls this metric, “one of the best indicators of the depth of our client relationships and the scale of the reinvention programs we are helping deliver.”

These are not small, discretionary projects that get shelved at the first sign of economic trouble. A nine-figure deal is a multi-year commitment to a fundamental business overhaul – think AI integration, data infrastructure, and core process reinvention. Securing these contracts embeds Accenture within a client’s long-term strategy, creating a durable stream of high-value work.

This area is central to the business. While overall revenue growth may be modest, the accelerating pace of these large-scale deals provides a foundation for the business. It signals that even in a cautious environment, some of the world’s largest companies are not pausing their critical transformations, and they are choosing Accenture for these projects.

sum: - Analyst Consensus: 14 Buys / 4 Outperforms / 10 Holds / 1 Underperform / 1 Sell
Accenture plc (ACN) is a global professional services company that helps large enterprises transform their operations through technology, AI integration, and managed services.
Accenture stock has been cut nearly in half from its 52-week high of $325.71, yet the underlying business just posted its strongest bookings quarter in company history.
Q2 fiscal 2026 revenue came in at $18.04 billion, up 8.3% year-over-year, landing at the top end of the company’s guided range.
New bookings hit a record $22.1 billion for the quarter, pushing first-half bookings to $43 billion and giving the company its third consecutive quarter above the $20 billion mark.

A record 41 clients booked more than $100 million in a single quarter, up from the low-30s range just a year ago, a figure CEO Julie Sweet described as direct evidence of “the continued demand for reinvention at scale.”
Sweet went further on the AI demand picture, telling investors: “AI, as it stands right now, may turn out to be the most powerful technology breakthrough since electricity.”
